messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 77
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Tutor
  trauma_type: Civilian in war zone
  pcl5: 55

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Stay Near Exit: make sure to stay close to exit, Avoid Media: Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events, Past Dwelling: I dwell on how I used to be before the event
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now., Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
  Negative Appraisals: Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside, Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it, Weakness Belief: I am a weak person

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Layla, at seventy-seven, carried a stillness that seemed out of place in the cheerful, cluttered homes where she tutored children in mathematics. The trauma was from a lifetime ago, another country, but its architecture remained, structuring her days. It happened during the war, on an afternoon that had felt deceptively ordinary. She had been in a small bakery, the air thick with the scent of cardamom, when the world outside the shop window dissolved into a cascade of white light and roaring sound. The building across the street collapsed into a cloud of dust and debris, the shockwave shattering the bakery’s windows and throwing her to the floor amidst the broken glass and scattered pastries. She remembers the screaming, the sudden darkness as the dust blotted out the sun, and a profound, animal terror that she was about to be buried alive.

In the years since resettling in America, that moment has never truly ended. She describes how something as simple as a car backfiring or a dropped crate at the grocery store can instantly bring back the full memory, not as a recollection, but as a lived reality. When this happens, she feels the same raw terror she felt on the bakery floor, a certainty that her life is ending. It is not like watching a film of the past; she feels the grit of dust in her mouth and the paralyzing fear that the ceiling is about to give way. This is why she has come to believe, with unshakeable conviction, that she is a weak person. The strength and resilience she once prided herself on feel like a memory of someone else. Now, she is certain that if she allows herself to truly think about the event, to let the memories in voluntarily, she will not be able to handle it. She imagines a complete shattering, a loss of self from which she would never return.

This core belief that she is too fragile to cope governs her every move. At the homes of her students, she will politely but firmly insist on being seated in the chair closest to the front door, ensuring her path to an exit is always clear. Her students’ parents see it as a quirk of an elderly woman, but for Layla, it is a non-negotiable condition for her safety. She has also systematically purged her life of potential reminders. She never watches the news or reads the paper, and if a film on television so much as hints at conflict or disaster, she immediately turns it off. This avoidance extends to her inner world; she spends hours dwelling on how she used to be before the event, looking at old photographs of a vibrant, smiling woman she no longer recognizes as herself. This rumination on a lost past is her safest way of touching her own history without getting too close to the part that burned it all down.

The conviction that her memories are unmanageable has, paradoxically, given them more power. Because she regards any flicker of the trauma as a sign of imminent collapse, the memories themselves arrive steeped in a secondary layer of terror. The thought “I can’t handle this” is the usher that announces their arrival, and this anticipatory dread makes the reliving experience feel even more vivid and threatening, confirming her belief that the memory itself is dangerous. The strategies she uses to protect herself also conspire against her. By refusing to watch news of current events or read about similar tragedies, she prevents herself from ever contextualizing her experience. As a result, when a sudden noise triggers a flashback, it comes without warning, a raw sensory fragment untethered to any narrative. The memory crashes into her consciousness with the full force of the original event precisely because she has worked so hard to keep the door to that part of her mind sealed.

This cycle of avoidance and intrusion has become the central proof of her own perceived weakness. Each time she has to reposition a chair to be near a door, she feels a hot flush of shame, a confirmation that she is no longer a capable person. Each evening she spends avoiding television and instead dwelling on the past reinforces the chasm between who she was and the frightened woman she has become. Her strategies are no longer just about safety; they are a constant, running commentary on her own inadequacy. This has left her with a pervasive feeling of being dead inside, a profound emotional numbness that blankets everything. It is this feeling, more than the fear, that finally brought her to therapy. The thick pane of glass between herself and the world has become unbearable. She is terrified of revisiting the memory, but the thought of living out the rest of her years as a ghost in her own life has become, at last, even more frightening.
